The Southworth name reached Plymouth by a wedding.
Alice Carpenter of Wrington in Somerset had married Edward Southworth among the English Separatists at Leiden in 1613,
and was left a widow with two small boys.
In the summer of 1623 she crossed on the ship Anne, and within weeks she married William Bradford,
the governor, whose first wife had drowned off Cape Cod in the Mayflower’s first month at anchor.
An English visitor, Emmanuel Altham, described the feast in a letter home: “Massasoit was sent for to the wedding,
where came with him his wife, the queen, although he hath five wives.
With him came four other kings and about six score men with their bows and arrows”.
The Wampanoag sachem “brought the Governor three or four bucks and a turkey”, and the company sat down to “about twelve
pasty venisons” and “other such good cheer”.
Alice’s sons followed her over within a few years and grew up in the governor’s house.
Constant, the elder, married Elizabeth Collier in 1637, settled at Duxbury near the Aldens,
and served the colony as treasurer and assistant.
In 1680 his son William married Rebecca Pabodie, John and Priscilla Alden’s granddaughter,
and the two lines became one. When Alice died in 1670 the colony’s record called her “a godly matron”.
